KEY MESSAGE 1...As of 12:50 AM EST...Sfc analysis shows a 1026 
mb sfc high centered almost directly overhead, with latest 
satellite imagery showing clear skies across the region. This 
has allowed temperatures to effectively radiate for many 
locations, high terrain areas mainly in the upper 20s to mid 
30s and mainly upper 30s to 40s in the valleys. Temperatures 
will drop a few to several more degrees before sunrise with some
patchy fog in some of the typical river valley areas and near 
wetlands. Tomorrow, clear skies in the morning give way to a few
more afternoon cirrus clouds as our next weather system begins 
to move up the coast. We will remain under the influence of an 
amplifying upper ridge, and given that the NBM has been running 
a few degrees too cool with daytime highs in this pattern, we 
bumped up highs tomorrow into the upper 50s to low 60s. With 
more clouds around, tomorrow night will be a few to several 
degrees warmer than tonight. Dry weather continues into Sunday 
morning.

Attention then turns to a coastal storm that still looks to bring 
some rain to the region late Sunday or Sunday night into Monday. As 
this storm moves up the coast, it will bring with it a plume of 
anomalous moisture. Forcing for ascent on the NW side of the storm 
still looks impressive with strong low-level warm advection and a 
band of FGEN, as well as some enhanced forcing from the right 
entrance region of the upper jet to our north. Rain likely begins 
Sunday evening. The heaviest rain will be Sunday night, tapering to 
showers Monday morning. 

Most of the 18 and 00z guidance continues to trend further east with 
this storm. Most guidance now shows the solution first 
advertised by yesterday's 12z Euro and 00z GFS. With this 
solution, an area of vorticity along a stalled frontal boundary 
east of Florida does not fully "wrap up", but instead 2 
separate centers of low pressure form near the front. The first 
sfc low (which yesterday looked like the primary low that would 
move up the coast) now looks to be weaker and track more inland 
near the FL/GA/SC coast, while a second area of low pressure to 
the east actually becomes the more dominant sfc low as it tracks
up the coast. This is likely due to upper-level ridging east of
Florida currently being a tad stronger and further west than 
previously modeled, which is nudging the initial sfc low a 
little further to the west/inland over the southeast US than 
what most guidance showed yesterday. 

We mentioned yesterday that such an outcome would result in a sfc 
low track further to the east as the storm moves off the southern 
New England coast, which is indeed what we have seen in most model 
guidance over the last 12 hrs or so. With this shift towards the 
east in the expected storm track, the axis of heaviest rainfall will 
likely end up to the east of our area, across southern New England. 
Guidance has also trended just a tad slower with the approaching 
cold front and upper trough to our west. This will result in a 
little more separation between the deep tropical moisture and best 
upper-level mid-latitude forcing. While some interaction with the 
mid-latitude jet still looks likely, these trends have decreased the 
chances for a PRE to occur. These trends have pretty 
significantly increased our confidence that we will not see any 
flooding issues. The fact that this storm will be fast-moving 
will also help reduce the duration of any heavier rainfall 
rates. 

However, there is still some uncertainty in exactly how far west the 
higher rainfall totals will extend. With a sharp qpf gradient on the 
western side of the storm, even minor changes to the storm track 
could result in rather large changes to qpf across our southeastern 
areas. Some of the latest 00z guidance is quite a bit further 
east with the qpf shield. Given the run-to-run changes we've 
seen over the past few days, we aren't quite ready to make 
wholesale changes to the forecast yet, but if this trend further
east continues then we may need to lower qpf amounts quite a 
bit with subsequent forecast updates. Ensemble sensitivity 
analysis shows that the forecast uncertainty is tied to the 
evolution of the two sfc lows east of Florida and the amplitude 
and east-west phase shift of the upstream trough. We should 
hopefully get a better handle on this system over the next 24 
hrs or so as these features evolve. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...Monday evening and night, a fairly strong cold front 
will move through the region. In its wake, some gusty W/NW winds 
will be possible. With the colder airmass moving over the Great 
Lakes, a few lake effect snow showers will be possible for western 
areas Monday night into Tuesday, but at this time any accumulations 
within our CWA look pretty light. High pressure then slides overhead 
Tuesday night and Wednesday, resulting in tranquil but chilly 
weather.
